title: ruff
text:
Configuration
Create a file named pyproject.toml with the following content. You can find the relevant rules here.
[tool.ruff]
target-version = "py39"

# Select relevant rules
select = [
    "ANN", # type annotations
    "ARG", # falke8 unused arguments
    "B",  # flake8-bugbear
    "COM", # flake8-commas (specifically trailing commas)
    "C4", # flake8-comprehensions
    "D",  # pydocstyle
    "E",  # Error
    "ERA", # eradicate commented out code
    "F",  # pyflakes
    "FIX", # flake8 fixme
    "I",  # isort
    "ISC", # flake8-implicit-str-concat
    "N",  # pep8-naming
    "NPY", # NumPy specific rules
    "PERF", # Perflint: performance
    "PIE", # flake8-pie 
    "PGH",  # pygrep-hooks
    "PTH", # flake8-use-pathlib 
    "Q",  # flake8-quotes
    "RUF", # Ruff specific rules
    "S",  # bandit security checks 
    "SIM",  # flake8-simplify
    "UP",  # pyupgrade
    "W",  # Warning
    "YTT", # flake8-2020 
]


# Ignore the following rules
ignore = [
    "ANN101", # missing-type-self
    "ANN401", # any-type type hint
    "D100", # undocumented-public-module
    "D101", # undocumented-public-class -> We document inits
    "D104", # Missing docstring in public package
    "E402", # (import violation)
]

line-length = 88  # Must agree with Black

[tool.ruff.per-file-ignores]
"path/to/python-file.py" = ["E501"] # line too long 
"path/to_test_folder/*" = [
    "ANN201", # Missing return type -> Tests commonly return None (overkill)
    "ANN202", # Missing return type -> Tests commonly return None (overkill)
    "D102", # No docstrings -> not necessary in tests
] 

# Doc-String format
[tool.ruff.pydocstyle]
convention = "google"  # Accepts: "google", "numpy", or "pep257".

title: Flutter
text:
Flutter

Architecture of a Flutter app
Everything in Flutter is a widget and you build widgets upon widgets like lego-blocks. In a new app you create a Scaffold. Within the Scaffold you can create e.g. an AppBar and a Container for the body of your app. This Container can contain a Column that contains widgets that stack vertically or a Row that contains widgets that get aligned horizontally. This creates a widget tree.
                Scaffold
                /      \
          AppBar        Container
                            \
                            Column
                                \
                             other widget
The information, where your widget is located in the widget tree is saved in the BuildContext. Every build function needs a BuildContext, to save where the widget goes.

The boilerplate stuff
First you import the packages i.e. for the style sheets:
import 'package:flutter/material.dart';
Then you define the main function (the starting point of your app):
void main() {
  runApp( // starts your app
    MaterialApp( // defines the style sheets that you can use
      home: Scaffold( // organizes layout of your app
        body: Text("Hello World"),
      ),
    ),
  );
}


Scaffold
The Scaffold is used to organize the layout of your (material) app and contains the widgets. These are the common components
home: Scaffold(
        appBar: AppBar(...),
        body: Text("Hello World"),
        floatingActionButton: FloatingActionButton(...),
        drawer: Drawer(...), //menu that you can pull in from the side
        bottomNavigationBar: BottomNavigationBar(...)
      )

<img src=“/img/Scaffold.png”, height=500px>




AppBar
AppBars are usually title bars in your app that also contain iconButtons.
AppBar(
       title: const Text('test'),
       backgroundColor: Colors.blueGrey[900],
       actions: <Widget>[ // action that happens when you click on the button
          IconButton(icon: const Icon(Icons.add_alert),
                     onPressed: () {...}
       )


Image
You can integrate Images from different sources by using different image objects from different parent classes.
Image( // displays content from image class
    image:NetworkImage('https://api.flutter.dev/flutter/widgets/Image-class.html'), // displays image from network
)
If you load images from your image assets folder, you need to change the pubspec.yaml file in your project’s root directory. Under assets you need to add the relative location of your image:
flutter:
  uses-material-design: true
  assets:
    - images/


Container
A container is a layout box that you can position and fill with content.
Container(
    color: Colors.white,
    child: Text("Hallo"), 
    width: 50, 
    height: 50,
    margin: EdgeInsets.all(20), // the margin on all 4 sides to your container
    padding: EdgeInsets.fromLTRB(5, 5, 10, 10) // the padding of the content in your container
To add a background image, you can use the decoration parameter:
Container(
    decoration: BoxDecoration(
      image: DecorationImage(
        image: AssetImage("images/background.png"), 
        fit: BoxFit.cover),
      ),
    ...)


SafeArea
The SafeArea widget constraints its children to the area of the screen that is easily visible (not below the notch of the selfie-camera).
SafeArea(
    child: ...
)

Column and Row
Column and Row widgets organize their children vertically and horizontally respectively.
Column(
    children <Widget>: [
        Container(...),
        SizedBox(height:10), // This provides some spacing between the elements
        Container(...)
    ],
    mainAxisSize: MainAxisSize.min, // if you don't want it to spread across the whole height
    verticalDirection: VerticalDirection.up, // if the children should be ordered reversely
    mainAxisAlignment: MainAxisAlignment.end, // if you want the children to stack up from the bottom
    crossAxisAlignment: CrossAxisAlignment.stretch,  // this stretches the children to the width of the screen
)


Expanded
The expanded widget must be contained in a Column or a Row widget. If fills out the available space in its parent container.
Row(
  children: <Widget>[
    Expanded(
       child: Image(...)
    )
)


Padding
To add padding around another widget (e.g. that does not have a padding-attribute), you can use the padding widget:
Padding(
    child
    padding:
)


Button
If you use FlatButton, you can use an image as the child. This converts the image into a button. Buttons have an onPressed argument, which require a VoidCallback objects. These are functions without inputs and outputs.
FlatButton(
  onPressed: (){...} // The () contain the arguments (none) and the {} contain the body of the function
  child: ...
)


Slider
If you use a slider, you need to set its starting value, min and max. To be able to drag the slider around, you need to update the state of the slider:
double sliderVal = 20.0;
Slider(
  value: sliderVal,
  min: 10,
  max: 30,
  onChanged: (double newVal) {
    setState(() {
      sliderVal = mewVal;
    });
  }  
)


Visibility
You can conditionally show your buttons or contents using the Visibility widget:
Visibility(
  child: FlatButton(...),
  visible: true
)


Icons
Icons are accessible like this (check mark as example):
Icon(
  Icons.check
)



Custom widgets
The basic idea of widgets in flutter is composition: The widgets are composed of several simpler widgets that depend on one another (not inhereted). This is also how you’d make custom widgets.
class myOwnButton extends StatelessWidget {
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) {
    return RawMaterialButton(
     ... // here you combine/define what you want  
    );
  }
}


Gesture Detector
You can check if an widget got tapped, forcedPressed, doubletapped… with a Gesture Detector as a parent:
GestureDetector(
    onTap: () {
      setState(() {...});
    },
    child: ...


Theme
The coloring, fonts, styles throughout the app are defined in the ThemeData widget. You can switch themes
MaterialApp(
  theme:ThemeData.dark() //uses the standard dart theme
)
You can adapt the default themes
MaterialApp(
  theme.ThemeData.dark().copyWith(
    primaryColor: ...
  )
)
or you can define your own ones.
MaterialApp(
  theme: ThemeData(
    primaryColor: Colors.lightBlue,
    textTheme: textTheme(...) //Text has its own theme
    ...
  )
)
You can also use very detailed themes for other widgets. You do it by wrapping the widget in its theme:
SliderTheme(
  data: SliderTheme.of(context).copyWith(
    ... // adapt theme to your liking
  ),
  child: Slider(
    ... // define Slider min, max, onChanged...
  )
)


Creating App Icons
To create an app icon from an image file, go to www.appicon.co and have it transformed to different resolutions. For Android, you use the newly created “mipmap-…”-folders and replace the respecitve folders in “/android/app/src/main/res” with them. For iOS, you use the newly created folder “Assets.xcassets” and replace the folder “/ios/Runner/Assets.xcassets” with it.


Run the app on a physical device
To run your app on a physical iPhone or Android device, you can follow the steps on this flutter-webpage.

title: R basics
text:
Using R

In console





Use R in console / terminal: R
Type your code
Quit R in console: q()


Run R scripts from console/terminal

In console / terminal: Rscript myScript.R









Get help with functions and features





Help section on function
?functionName


Find functions / features matching a term
??TermOfInterest


List arguments that the function accepts
args(functionName)





File system, Import, Input, Output







Use file system





print working directory
getwd()


Change working directory
setwd("path/to/dir")


List files in working directory
dir()


Create directory
dir.create("path/to/dir", recursive=TRUE)


Create file
file.create("myfile.R")


Check if file exists
file.exists("myfile.R")


Get info on file (size, time of creation)
file.info("mytest.R")


Rename file
file.rename("mytest.R", "mytest2.R")


Copy file
file.copy("mytest2.R", "mytest3.R")


Construct file path from directory list
file.path("folder", "subfolder", "file") # "folder/subfolder/file




Importing other scripts




source("otherScript.R")
Executes the contents of the script.

Send all standard output to a file




sink("output.txt")

Print to standard output




print("my Output")


Operations, numbers, vectors, matrices







Assign values to a variable





Assign value to variable
x <- 4.5


Assign to multiple variables
x <- y <- z <- 4.5


Assign/change value of variable in global scope
x <<- "global value"




Create a vector




x <- c(10, 4.5, 12, 5)






Warning



!: If you integrate vectors in your vector ( c(10, c(11, 12), 13) ) it will get flattened (like c(10, 11, 12, 13) ).



Element-wise adding, subtracting, dividing, multiplying, … vectors




x <- c(1, 2)
y <- c(10, 11, 12, 13)
z <- x + y






Warning



You can make element-wise operations with vectors of different lengths, as long as the longer one is a multiple of the shorter one. The shorter vector is repeated. 😧









Common operators on vectors





maximum, minimum
max(x) min(x)


Vector of min and max
range(x)


Number of elements
length(x)


Sum of the elements
sum(x)


Product of the elements
prod(x)


Mean of the elements
mean(x)


Variance of the elements
var(x)


Sort elements ascending
sort(x)


Matrix multiplication
mat1 %*% mat2


Dimension of matrix
dim(mat1)


Number of rows
nrow(mat1)


Number of cols
ncol(mat2)


mode (highest count of val)
names(sort(-table(df$col1)))[1]


Percentile
quantile(df$col1, c(0.75))



!: If x is a n-by-p matrix, then var(x) will return a p-by-p covariance matrix.

Generate sequences




x <- c(1:10) # Integers from 1 to 10
# Or
x <- seq(1,10, 0.5) # 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, ...

text:
Dockerfile

BasicStaged


Dockerfile example:
1FROM rocker/shiny:latest
2RUN apt-get update
RUN apt-get install -qq -y libpq-dev
RUN install2.r ggplot2 shiny shinydashboard \
    shinydashboardPlus \
    dplyr RPostgres
3WORKDIR /srv/shiny-server
4COPY app/ .
5ENV R_VERSION=4.4.0
6EXPOSE 3838
7ENTRYPOINT ["R", "--vanilla"]
8CMD ["-e", "shiny::runApp('/srv/shiny-server', host='0.0.0.0', port=3838)"]
9HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost:3838/ || exit 1

1

FROM specifies the base image

2

RUN executes a command in the container

3

WORKDIR sets the working directory for all following instructions (like cd for the build)

4

COPY copies files from the build context (directory passed to docker build) into the image

5

ENV sets environment variables in the container (avoid secrets here; pass them at run time with -e or compose)

6

EXPOSE only documents which ports the container listens on; publishing to the host still requires -p

7

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable and fixed arguments when a container starts: here R with --vanilla (no saved workspace or startup profiles). The JSON (exec) form avoids an extra shell.

8

CMD supplies default arguments appended to ENTRYPOINT: here -e and the Shiny expression. Together they start the app directly in R instead of the base image’s Shiny Server. host='0.0.0.0' makes the app reachable through a published port. Without an ENTRYPOINT, CMD would need to specify the executable too.

9

HEALTHCHECK runs a command periodically (here every 30s) and marks the container unhealthy after repeated failures; the status shows up in docker ps. Requires curl in the image. Its CMD is separate from the container’s startup CMD and does not use ENTRYPOINT.




Example of a multi-stage Python Dockerfile: install dependencies in a build stage, then copy only the virtual environment and application into the runtime image. This makes the image smaller (faster deploys, less regisry storage, smaller attack surface).
# ---- Build stage: install dependencies with uv ----
1FROM ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.13-bookworm-slim AS build

ENV UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 \
2    UV_LINK_MODE=copy

WORKDIR /app

COPY pyproject.toml uv.lock ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/uv \
3    uv sync --locked --no-install-project --no-dev

# ---- Runtime stage: slim Python, app + venv only ----
4FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm

WORKDIR /app

5COPY --from=build /app/.venv /app/.venv
6COPY --chmod=644 main.py backend.py ui.py ./

RUN mkdir -p /data /opt/app-home \
    && chgrp -R 0 /data /opt/app-home \
7    && chmod -R g=u /data /opt/app-home

8USER 1001:0

9EXPOSE 3838

10CMD ["/app/.venv/bin/python", "main.py"]

1

Base image with UV, python13 and slimmed down Debian OS (saves space); AS build lets later instructions copy files from this stage.

2

Configure uv: UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 compiles installed Python files to bytecode during the build, which can improve startup time. UV_LINK_MODE=copy copies packages from uv’s cache into the virtual environment instead of linking them, keeping the environment independent of the cache mount.

3

Install dependencies into /app/.venv. --locked to adhere to lock-file. --no-install-project skips installing your own project as a package; --no-dev excludes the dev dependency group. The BuildKit cache mount reuses uv downloads across builds. This cache is not included in the image.

4

Start a fresh runtime stage with Python, using the same Python version and Debian release for compatibility.

5

Copy the installed virtual environment from build, keeping its absolute path unchanged because installed scripts can reference that path.

6

Copy the application scripts from the build context into /app. Permission mode 644 allows owner to read and write, and everyone else to read. The files remain root-owned, but the application user can read them; executable permission is unnecessary because Python runs them.

7

This command creates two directories (/data and /opt/app-home), sets their group ownership to root (GID 0), and ensures group permissions match user permissions (g=u).

8

Run subsequent instructions and the container’s default command as the default non-root user (UID=1001), 0 sets group to root group (not the same as root permissions).

9

Document that the application listens on port 3838. Publish it with docker run -p 3838:3838 ... or Compose’s ports; the application must also listen on 0.0.0.0, not just 127.0.0.1.

10

Start main.py with the virtual environment’s Python interpreter. Using its absolute path avoids needing to activate the environment or modify PATH. The JSON (exec) form avoids an extra shell and lets Python receive container signals directly.

WarningArgument order matters





Arguments after the image name replace the entire CMD. - docker run -rm -p 3838:3838 my-shiny-app keeps the default CMD. - docker run -rm my-shiny-app -e 'seesionInfo()' replaces the entire CMD but keeps the ENTRYPOINT resulting in e.g. R --vanilla -e 'sessionInfo()'.




Useful Options

Option
Description

Automatically remove the container when it exits

title: Docker
text:
Docker Compose
Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications using a YAML file.
Example docker-compose.yml:
services:
  postgres:
    container_name: db_container
1    build: ./postgres
    restart: always
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=postgres
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=postgres
    ports:
2      - "5432:5432"
    volumes:
3      - "postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"
  
  shiny:
    container_name: shiny
    depends_on:
      - postgres
    build: ./shiny
    volumes:
4      - "./shiny-logs:/var/log/shiny-server"
      - "./shiny-home:/srv/shiny-server"
    ports:
      - "3838:3838"
5    cpus: 1.5
    mem_limit: 2g
    memswap_limit: 2g
6    init: true

volumes:
7  postgres_data:

1

build points to the folder that contains the Dockerfile for this service; compose builds the image from it (alternative: image: to pull a ready-made image from a registry)

2

ports maps host:container — traffic on host port 3838 is forwarded to container port 3838

3

volumes here maps volume-name:container-path. Docker creates and manages the named volume for you. It survives the container removal. It must be declared at the bottom (7).

4

volumes here maps host-path:container-path — a folder next to the docker-compose.yml on the host is mounted into the container (equivalent to -v); data survives container removal

5

Resource limits the container can use: mem_limit: maximum RAM. memswap_limit: maximum RAM + swap to disk (can avoid OOM errors).

6

init: true For apps spawning subprocesses: Runs a lightweight init process as PID 1, forwards signals to the application and reaps exited orphaned child processes.

7

Declaration of the named volumes that are used above.



Starting and Recreating Containers
Start all services in the background:
docker compose up -d
Normally, up recreates existing containers only when their configuration or image has changed. --force-recreate replaces them even if nothing changed.


Useful Compose Options
These options belong to docker compose up and can be combined, e.g. docker compose up -d --build:







Option
Description




-d, --detach
Run containers in the background


--build
Build service images before starting containers; uses the build cache


--no-build
Do not build images; required images must already exist or be pulled


--pull always
Pull service images from the registry before running (missing and never are other policies)


--force-recreate
Replace containers even if their configuration and image have not changed


--no-recreate
Keep existing containers even if configuration or images changed; incompatible with --force-recreate


--no-deps
Do not start dependencies of the selected services, e.g. docker compose up -d --no-deps shiny


--wait
Wait until services are running or healthy; implies detached mode. Define health checks to verify readiness


--wait-timeout 60
Limit the wait for readiness to 60 seconds



Global options go before the subcommand:







Option
Description




-f <file>
Select a Compose file; repeat to merge files in order, e.g. docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d


-p <name>
Set the project name to separate application stacks


--env-file <file>
Load variables from referenced xxx.env-file. Variables are only used if referenced in compose file (e.g. name: "${NAME_FROM_ENV_FILE}")


--profile <name>
Enable services assigned to a profile, e.g. docker compose --profile debug up -d if these services in the compose file have a field profiles: ["debug"]





Other Useful Compose Commands







Command
Description




docker compose ps -a
Show all service containers, including stopped ones


docker compose logs -f --tail=100
Follow logs for all services; append a service name to filter


docker compose exec shiny /bin/bash
Open a shell in the running shiny service; use /bin/sh if Bash is unavailable


docker compose run --rm shiny <command>
Run a one-off command in a new container and remove it afterward; service ports are not published by default


docker compose config
Render and validate the resolved Compose configuration


docker compose pull
Pull service images without replacing running containers; follow with up -d to apply them


docker compose build --no-cache
Build images without cached layers; add --pull to also check for newer base images


docker compose stop
Stop containers without removing them


docker compose down
Stop and remove service containers and project networks; keep volumes by default


docker compose down -v
Also remove declared named volumes and attached anonymous volumes; deletes their data. External volumes and bind-mounted host files are not removed



See the Docker CLI reference for compose up and compose down.

title: Pydantic
text:
Models and constraints
from typing import Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict, Field

class Message(BaseModel):
    role: Literal["system", "user", "assistant"]
    content: str = Field(min_length=1)

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")  # reject unknown keys

    messages: list[Message] = Field(min_length=1)  # nested validation
    temperature: float = Field(default=0.7, ge=0, le=2)
    max_tokens: int = Field(default=512, gt=0, le=4096)
    user_id: str | None = None
    metadata: dict[str, str] = Field(default_factory=dict)

request = ChatRequest(messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}])
request.messages[0].content  # "Hello"; nested dict becomes a Message







Declaration
Meaning




name: str
Required, cannot be None


name: str \| None
Required, but accepts None


name: str \| None = None
May be omitted or None


tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
New empty list per instance




Constraints: gt / ge / lt / le for numbers; min_length / max_length for strings and collections; pattern for regex matching on strings.
Coercion is on by default: an int field accepts "512". Use Field(strict=True) per field or ConfigDict(strict=True) model-wide to disable coercion.
Extra keys are ignored by default. Use extra="forbid" to catch misspelled inputs.
Defaults are not validated by default. Enable validate_default=True in Field or ConfigDict when needed.

title: Pydantic
text:
FastAPI request and response
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    tokens_used: int = Field(ge=0)

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat(body: ChatRequest):
    # Replace with your model call; return a model or a dict, not JSON text.
    return ChatResponse(answer="Hello!", tokens_used=3)

Invalid request data → automatic 422 response; no manual parsing needed.
response_model validates, documents, and filters the output to declared fields. Use separate input/output models to keep internal fields out of responses.
Invalid response data is a server bug → 500 by default, not 422.

title: Pydantic
text:
Validate and serialize







Operation
Pydantic v2




Python dict → model
ChatRequest.model_validate(data)


JSON string/bytes → model
ChatRequest.model_validate_json(raw)


Model → Python dict (nested models included)
request.model_dump()


Model → JSON-compatible dict (dates, UUIDs, etc.)
request.model_dump(mode="json")


Model → JSON string
request.model_dump_json()


Model → JSON Schema
ChatRequest.model_json_schema()


Only explicitly supplied fields (e.g. PATCH)
request.model_dump(exclude_unset=True)


Omit None values
request.model_dump(exclude_none=True)



exclude_unset=True preserves an explicitly supplied None; exclude_none=True removes it. For PATCH, define a separate update model with omittable fields.
Aliases: Field(alias="maxTokens") accepts an external key; model_dump(by_alias=True) emits it. ORM objects: use ConfigDict(from_attributes=True) with model_validate(obj).

title: Pydantic
Pydantic
text:
Structured LLM output
Reuse a model as the output contract and validate the LLM’s JSON at the boundary:
from pydantic import ValidationError

class Classification(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid")
    label: Literal["positive", "negative", "neutral"]
    confidence: float = Field(ge=0, le=1)

schema = Classification.model_json_schema()  # for provider schema/tool APIs
raw = '{"label":"positive","confidence":0.95}'  # example LLM output
try:
    result = Classification.model_validate_json(raw)
except ValidationError as exc:
    errors = exc.errors()  # structured errors: loc, msg, type, etc.
    # Reject or retry with feedback; avoid logging sensitive input.
Schema-valid output is not necessarily factually correct or safe. Providers support different JSON Schema subsets; prefer their SDK’s Pydantic integration when available. model_validate_json expects JSON, not Markdown fences or surrounding prose.

title: Pydantic
text:
App settings
Settings live in the separate pydantic-settings package (uv add pydantic-settings):
from pydantic import SecretStr
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", extra="ignore")
    model_api_key: SecretStr  # reads MODEL_API_KEY from the environment
    model_name: str = "my-model"

settings = Settings()  # load once, not on every request
# settings.model_api_key.get_secret_value() when calling the provider
SecretStr masks normal display; it does not encrypt secrets. Never return settings from an endpoint or commit .env files.

title: Pydantic
text:
Avoid these traps

Old v1 examples: use model_dump() / model_dump_json() / model_validate() instead of .dict() / .json() / .parse_obj().
model_construct() skips validation; model_copy(update=...) does not validate updates. Revalidate untrusted merged data with Model.model_validate(...).
Validating a model does not validate later attribute assignments unless validate_assignment=True is configured.

title: FastAPI
text:
FastAPI is a Python framework for building APIs, built on Starlette.
Starlette is the web framework that provides FastAPI’s routing and web functionality.
Pydantic validates and serializes data using Python type hints.
ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is a standard interface between asynchronous Python web applications and servers.

title: FastAPI
text:
FastAPI is a Python framework for building APIs, built on Starlette.
Starlette is the web framework that provides FastAPI’s routing and web functionality.
Pydantic validates and serializes data using Python type hints.
ASGI (Asynchronous Server Gateway Interface) is a standard interface between asynchronous Python web applications and servers.
Uvicorn is an ASGI server that runs FastAPI and Starlette applications and handles incoming connections.

title: FastAPI
text:
Installation and Setup

Installation
Use uv to install FastAPI with its standard dependencies, including the FastAPI CLI and Uvicorn:
uv add "fastapi[standard]"


Creating an application
Create main.py in the project root or ./app directory:
from fastapi import FastAPI

1app = FastAPI()

2@app.get("/")
async def root():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}

1

Creates the ASGI application that receives requests.

2

Registers a handler function for GET /; its return value is sent as JSON.




Configure and run
Add the application entrypoint to pyproject.toml so the FastAPI CLI knows where to find it:
[tool.fastapi]
1entrypoint = "main:app"

1

main:app means the object app in the Python module main (main.py). For an application in app/main.py, use app.main:app instead.


Run from the project root:
uv run fastapi dev             # development: automatic reload, localhost only
uv run fastapi run             # production mode: no reload, listens on 0.0.0.0

title: FastAPI
text:
Routing and Path Operations

HTTP Methods and Routes
Routes: A path operation connects an HTTP method and a URL path to a handler function. The same path can have different handlers for different methods.
Routers: Use APIRouter to group related routes:
from fastapi import APIRouter, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()
1router = APIRouter(prefix="/items", tags=["items"])
items = []

2@router.get("/")
async def list_items():
    return items

3@router.post("/", status_code=201)
async def create_item():
    new_item = {"id": len(items) + 1, "name": "Example", "price": 10.0}
    items.append(new_item)
    return new_item

4app.include_router(router)

1

Groups routes under /items with a shared documentation tag; routers can also share dependencies.

2

Handle GET /items/.

3

Handle POST /items/; status_code=201 sets the success response code.

4

Registers the router’s endpoints with the application. Routers can live in separate files: see the example file structure.


Other decorators include @router.put(...), @router.patch(...), and @router.delete(...); the same decorators are available directly on app. See HTTP methods.
FastAPI evaluates routes in declaration order: declare a fixed path like /users/me before /users/{user_id} so it is not captured as a user ID.

title: FastAPI
text:
Handling requests



Declaration
Read from




Name appears in the route’s {braces}
Path


Scalar type, such as str, int, or bool
Query string


Pydantic model, dict, list
JSON body




Path and Query Parameters
Names in {braces} are taken from the path; other scalar function parameters are normally taken from the query string. Type hints control parsing and validation:
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(
1    item_id: int,
2    q: str,
3    limit: int = 10,
4    details: bool = False,
):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q, "limit": limit, "details": details}

1

item_id is a required path parameter, parsed as an integer.

2

q is a required query parameter because it has no default.

3

limit is an optional query parameter, parsed as an integer and defaulting to 10.

4

details is an optional query parameter, parsed as a boolean and defaulting to False.


To allow an omitted query parameter to be None, use e.g. q: str | None = None.
For additional constraints on parameter values, see Type Hints and Validation Constraints.

title: FastAPI
text:
Request Data and Validation

Pydantic Models and Request Bodies
Declare a Pydantic model to receive a JSON request body. FastAPI parses the JSON, validates it, and passes a model instance to the handler:
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI()

class Item(BaseModel):
1    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)
    price: float = Field(gt=0)
2    description: str | None = None
3    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

@app.post("/items", status_code=201)
4async def create_item(item: Item):
5    return item.model_dump()

1

Fields without defaults are required. Field adds validation constraints and schema metadata.

2

Allows a string or None; the default None also allows the field to be omitted. str | None without a default would still require the field.

3

Creates a new empty list when tags is omitted. Collections and nested Pydantic models are validated recursively.

4

A Pydantic model parameter is read from the request body, not the query string.

5

Access values with e.g. item.name; model_dump() converts the model to a dictionary.


Example request body (send with Content-Type: application/json):
{"name": "Notebook", "price": 4.5, "tags": ["office"]}


Type Hints and Validation Constraints
Type hints define accepted data types; Field (for Pydantic), Path, Query, and Body add constraints and documentation. Use Annotated to attach type-metadata that fastAPI uses for validation:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Path, Query

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(
1    item_id: Annotated[int, Path(ge=1)],
2    limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10,
):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "limit": limit}

1

Path(ge=1) requires an integer greater than or equal to 1.

2

Query(ge=1, le=100) restricts the query parameter to 1–100; its default remains 10.


Common validation constraints:








Constraint
Meaning
Example




gt, ge
Greater than / greater than or equal to
Field(gt=0)


lt, le
Less than / less than or equal to
Query(le=100)


min_length, max_length
Bounds on string or collection length
Field(min_length=1)


pattern
Regular expression for a string
Query(pattern=r"^[a-z]+$")



For a scalar body value, use Body explicitly; otherwise FastAPI normally treats a scalar as a query parameter:

Single Body ParameterMultiple Body Parameters


A single scalar body parameter normally expects the model’s fields directly: {"price": 4.5, "name": "notebook"}
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Body

@app.put("/items/{item_id}/price")
async def update_price(
    item_id: int,
1    price: Annotated[float, Body(gt=0, embed=True)],
):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "price": price}

1

embed=True expects {"price": 4.5} rather than a bare JSON number 4.5.


Expected body: {"price": 4.5}.


Multiple body parameters are wrapped under their parameter names {"price": 4.5, "item": {"name": "Notebook", "item_id": 4}}.
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Body
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=80)
    price: float = Field(gt=0)
    description: str | None = None
    tags: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

@app.put("/items/{item_id}/price")
async def update_price(
    item_id: int,
    price: Annotated[float, Body(gt=0)],
    item: Item,
):
    return {"device price": item.price, "total price": price}
Expected body: {"price": 4.5, "item": {"name": "Notebook", "price": 4.5, "tags": ["portable"]}}.





Headers and Cookies
Use Header and Cookie to read these values instead of query parameters:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Cookie, Header

@app.get("/preferences")
async def read_preferences(
1    user_agent: Annotated[str | None, Header()] = None,
2    theme: Annotated[str, Cookie()] = "light",
):
    return {"user_agent": user_agent, "theme": theme}

1

Reads the User-Agent header: Header converts underscores to hyphens by default, and header names are case-insensitive. Use Header(alias="User-Agent") to specify a header name explicitly.

2

Reads the theme cookie, defaulting to "light" if absent. Omit the default to make a header or cookie required.




Forms and File Uploads
Use Form for form fields and File / UploadFile for uploaded files.
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import File, Form, UploadFile

@app.post("/uploads")
async def upload_file(
1    file: Annotated[UploadFile, File()],
2    description: Annotated[str, Form(max_length=200)] = "",
):
3    contents = await file.read()
    return {
        "filename": file.filename,
        "description": description,
        "size_bytes": len(contents),
    }

1

UploadFile uses a spooled file (memory, then disk above a size threshold), so it can handle larger uploads without immediately loading them into memory. Access metadata with file.filename and file.content_type. Annotated[bytes, File()] instead loads the entire file into memory; list[UploadFile] accepts multiple files.

2

Reads a form field from the same request. Forms without files normally use application/x-www-form-urlencoded; uploads use multipart/form-data.

3

Reads the entire file contents as bytes, so this is suitable for small files. Decode text with contents.decode("utf-8"). For large files, repeatedly call await file.read(size) to process chunks instead of loading everything into memory. FastAPI closes files automatically at request cleanup.








WarningForm/File or JSON-Body





Form/file parameters cannot share the same request body with ordinary JSON body parameters. Use form fields for accompanying data rather than expecting a separate JSON body.

title: FastAPI
text:
Responses

Response Models and Serialization
response_model validates, documents, and filters output to the declared fields. FastAPI serializes models, dates, and UUIDs to JSON automatically:
from pydantic import BaseModel

class UserOut(BaseModel):
    name: str

@app.get("/users/me", response_model=UserOut)
async def read_user():
    return {"name": "Ada", "password_hash": "hidden"}  # Only name is sent.
A return annotation such as -> UserOut also use the response model (then the type of the response must be UserOut however); explicit response_model takes priority. Use response_model_exclude_none=True to omit None fields.


Status Codes, Headers, and Cookies
Set the default success status in the decorator; inject Response (from server) to modify headers, cookies, or response.status_code dynamically:
from fastapi import Response, status

@app.post("/preferences", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
1async def save_preferences(response: Response, theme: str):
    response.headers["X-App-Version"] = "1"
2    response.set_cookie("theme", theme, httponly=True, secure=True, samesite="lax")
    return {"saved": True}

@app.delete("/preferences", status_code=status.HTTP_204_NO_CONTENT)
async def clear_preferences():
3    response = Response(status_code=204)
4    response.delete_cookie("theme")
    return response

1

Response is not provided by the client, but injected from the server.

2

Cookie security flags:

3

Creates the actual response to return, rather than using an injected response.

4

Expires the browser’s cookie. If it was set with a custom path or domain, use the same values when deleting it.




Custom and Streaming Responses
For custom responses, use classes from fastapi.responses: HTMLResponse, PlainTextResponse, RedirectResponse, or FileResponse(path, filename="download.csv").
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse, StreamingResponse

@app.get("/page", response_class=HTMLResponse)
async def page():
    return "<h1>Hello</h1>"

@app.get("/stream")
async def stream():
    return StreamingResponse(iter(["Hello\n", "World\n"]), media_type="text/plain")
StreamingResponse accepts a sync or async iterator of chunks. Returning a Response directly (instead of FastAPI constructing it) bypasses response-model validation and serialization. Using response_class or responses in the decorator documents the format, but it does not restore validation.

title: FastAPI
text:
Error Handling

HTTP Exceptions and Validation Errors
Raise, rather than return, HTTPException to stop a request:
from fastapi import HTTPException

@app.get("/items/{item_id}")
async def read_item(item_id: int):
    if item_id != 1:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Item not found")
    return {"id": item_id}
The error body is {"detail": "Item not found"}. FastAPI prodcues 422 automatically for invalid request data and 500 for invalid response data.


Custom Exception Handlers
Register a handler for an exception class to customize errors globally:
from fastapi import Request
from fastapi.exceptions import RequestValidationError
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

@app.exception_handler(RequestValidationError)
1async def validation_error(request: Request, exc: RequestValidationError):
    return JSONResponse(status_code=422, content={"detail": "Invalid request data"})

1

FastAPI requires the two arguments request (that caused the error) and exc (provides details on the error).

title: FastAPI
text:
Dependency Injection

Declaring and Reusing Dependencies
Depends calls a function and injects its result; dependencies can themselves depend on other dependencies:
from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, Query

def pagination(limit: Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] = 10):
    return {"limit": limit}

1Pagination = Annotated[dict, Depends(pagination)]

@app.get("/items")
2async def list_items(params: Pagination):
    return params

1

This is a type alias meaning: This value is a dictionary obtained by calling pagination. It does not call pagination directly.

2

FastAPI calls pagination with the limit parameter from the query string: Query: GET /items?limit=25. Response: {"limit": 25}.


Reuse the alias across endpoints. Results are cached per request by default (use_cache=False disables this).


Dependencies with Cleanup
Use a single yield and finally (or a context manager) to release resources even on errors:
from typing import Annotated, Literal, TextIO
from fastapi import Depends

1def get_file(filename: str):
    file = open(filename, encoding="utf-8")
    try:
        yield file
    finally:
        file.close()

@app.get("/files/{filename}")
2def read_file(file: Annotated[TextIO, Depends(get_file)]):
    return {"contents": file.read()}

1

FastAPI reads filename from the route’s path, even though it is declared in the dependency.

2

For GET /files/data.txt, FastAPI calls get_file(filename="data.txt") and injects the yielded file into read_file. The finally block closes it after use, including when the endpoint raises an exception.


Cleanup normally runs after the response is sent, including streaming; Depends(get_file, scope="function") cleans up before sending it.

title: FastAPI
text:
Security

Authentication and Authorization

Authentication verifies identity; authorization checks roles, ownership, or permissions. Enforce both in dependencies, not only in the UI.
Return 401 for missing/invalid credentials (WWW-Authenticate: Bearer for bearer auth); 403 for insufficient permissions.
Use HTTPS, hash passwords, and keep secrets outside source code. Validate JWT signatures, expiry, issuer, and audience; decoding alone is not validation.



OAuth2, Bearer Tokens, and API Keys
Security helpers from fastapi.security extract credentials and add OpenAPI security schemes:







Helper
Credentials




OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="token")
Bearer token; documents an OAuth2 password token endpoint


HTTPBearer()
Authorization: Bearer <token> as an HTTPAuthorizationCredentials object


APIKeyHeader(name="X-API-Key")
API key from a header



from typing import Annotated
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.security import HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, HTTPBearer

app = FastAPI()
1bearer = HTTPBearer()
2BearerCredentials = Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(bearer)]

@app.get("/auth-info")
async def auth_info(credentials: BearerCredentials):
3    return {"scheme": credentials.scheme}

1

HTTPBearer() creates a dependency that extracts bearer credentials from the Authorization header and adds a bearer security scheme to OpenAPI. It rejects missing or non-bearer credentials by default, but does not validate the token itself.

2

HTTPAuthorizationCredentials is the object holding the extracted authentication scheme and raw token. This alias tells FastAPI to call bearer and inject that object.

3

credentials.scheme contains "Bearer"; credentials.credentials contains the raw token.


Client sends Authorization: Bearer <token> to this endpoint.


CORS
CORS controls which browser origins (scheme + host + port) can access the API:
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["https://app.example.com"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["GET", "POST"],
    allow_headers=["Authorization", "Content-Type"],
)

title: FastAPI
text:
Application Lifecycle and Configuration

Lifespan Events
Use lifespan for shared resources: code before yield runs at startup, cleanup runs at shutdown.
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from fastapi import FastAPI
from httpx import AsyncClient

@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    async with AsyncClient() as client:
        app.state.http = client  # Reuse a connection pool across requests.
        yield
    # The context manager closes the client on shutdown.

app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)
Access the client through request.app.state.http in a handler that accepts request: Request. Lifespan runs separately in each worker process.


Settings and Environment Variables
Install with uv add pydantic-settings. Settings are typed and validated; environment variables override .env values, which override defaults:
from functools import lru_cache
from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(env_file=".env", env_prefix="APP_")
    debug: bool = False
    database_url: str  # Required: APP_DATABASE_URL.

1@lru_cache
def get_settings() -> Settings:
    return Settings()

1

The cache avoids re-reading configuration on every request.


Inject with settings: Annotated[Settings, Depends(get_settings)]. Keep .env and secrets out of version control; use environment injection or a secret manager in production.


Middleware
Middleware wraps requests and responses:
from time import perf_counter
from fastapi import Request
from loguru import logger

@app.middleware("http") # <1>
1async def log_timing(request: Request, call_next):
    start = perf_counter()
    response = await call_next(request)
    logger.info("Request completed in {:.6f} seconds", perf_counter() - start)
    return response

1

Middleware wraps all http requests for all routes and methods - but not websocket connections.


The last-added middleware runs first on requests and last on responses. Use app.add_middleware(...) for middleware classes, such as CORS.

title: FastAPI
text:
Testing

Test Client and Async Tests
Install with uv add --dev pytest httpx. Tests call the app directly without starting a server; run with uv run pytest:
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
from main import app

def test_root():
    with TestClient(app) as client:  # Context manager runs lifespan.
        response = client.get("/")
    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"message": "Hello World"}
For tests that need await, use HTTPX’s async client and AnyIO’s pytest plugin (AnyIO is a FastAPI dependency):
import pytest
from httpx import ASGITransport, AsyncClient
from main import app

@pytest.fixture
def anyio_backend():
    return "asyncio"

@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_root_async():
    async with AsyncClient(
        transport=ASGITransport(app=app), base_url="http://test"
    ) as client:
        response = await client.get("/")
    assert response.status_code == 200
ASGITransport does not run lifespan automatically. If startup resources are required, wrap the client in async with LifespanManager(app) from asgi-lifespan (uv add --dev asgi-lifespan).


Dependency Overrides
Map the original dependency function to a replacement, e.g. to swap settings, authentication, or database sessions:
from main import app, get_settings, Settings

def test_with_settings():
    app.dependency_overrides[get_settings] = lambda: Settings(
        database_url="sqlite://", debug=True
    )
    try:
        with TestClient(app) as client:
            assert client.get("/").status_code == 200
    finally:
        app.dependency_overrides.pop(get_settings, None)

Deployment and Observability

ASGI Servers and Production Configuration
Serve the ASGI app with Uvicorn (or another ASGI server, such as Hypercorn):
uv run uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --workers 4

Never use --reload in production; it cannot be combined with --workers.
Workers are separate processes: memory, caches, ML models, and connection pools are duplicated. Choose the count based on memory and load; orchestrated containers often use one worker per replica.
Put HTTPS termination/load balancing in front of the app and trust forwarded headers only from known proxies (--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips=...). Use --root-path /api if a proxy strips that URL prefix.
Configure restarts, health/readiness checks, resource limits, and graceful shutdown. Run migrations once before workers start, not independently in each worker’s lifespan.

title: HTTP & REST
text:
Debugging
Work through the layers: local process → DNS → TCP connection → TLS → HTTP → application. Start with the exact failing URL, method, headers and body; compare with server logs using the timestamp or request ID.

Local processes and ports
List processes with open network sockets, including listening sockets and connections (macOS / Linux with lsof installed).







Command
When to use it




lsof -i -P -n
List open network sockets (-i); keep ports (-P) and IP addresses (-n) numeric. COMMAND / PID identify the process; NAME shows addresses and ports. Omit -P for service names (e.g. https), which are port labels, not proof of the running application


lsof -nP -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN
Show TCP servers listening for connections: -iTCP selects TCP sockets; -sTCP:LISTEN filters for listening sockets


lsof -nP -iTCP:8000 -sTCP:LISTEN
Find the process listening on TCP port 8000; -iTCP:8000 restricts the selection to that port


ss -lntup
Linux alternative: show listening (-l) TCP (-t) and UDP (-u) sockets with numeric addresses/ports (-n) and process information (-p). UDP has no TCP-style LISTEN state




Address already in use — another process owns the port; identify it before stopping anything, or choose another port.
Connection refused — check that the server is running and listening on the expected port and interface.
A server bound to 127.0.0.1 is reachable only locally. Containers also need a published port; a service inside a container usually needs to bind to 0.0.0.0 (all IPv4 interfaces). Do not expose a development server publicly by accident by binding it to all host interfaces (0.0.0.0 or ::), publishing a container port on all host interfaces (e.g. docker run -p 8000:8000 …).



Inspect a response with curl







Command
When to use it




curl 'https://api.example.com/health'
GET request; prints the response body


curl -i 'https://api.example.com/health'
Include response status and headers with the body


curl -I 'https://api.example.com/health'
Send HEAD, not GET; some servers handle it differently or reject it


curl -v 'https://api.example.com/health'
Inspect connection details, TLS negotiation, request headers (>) and response headers (<); diagnostics go to stderr


curl -L --max-redirs 5 'https://api.example.com/health'
Follow redirects. If the destination is unexpected, run curl without -L first and inspect Location in the header to see where the original URL redirects to.


curl --compressed 'https://api.example.com/users'
Request a supported compressed response (E.g. gzip) and decompress it automatically


curl -sS -o response.json 'https://api.example.com/users'
 Stores errors in a JSON-file, hides the progress meter.


curl --trace-ascii trace.txt --trace-time
Get a .txt-file with detailed diagnostic trace (connection events, sent/received headers and data + timestamps).









WarningVerbose output and traces can expose tokens, cookies and personal data





redact before sharing and do not commit them.



By default, curl can exit successfully even for HTTP 404 or 500: the HTTP transfer itself succeeded. --fail-with-body makes HTTP errors return a nonzero exit code (usually 22) while keeping the error body.

Example response
Illustrative, shortened output from curl -v (exact wording depends on the curl version and TLS backend). The hostname and IP are placeholders; this example negotiates HTTP/1.1.

user ~ % curl -v 'https://api.example.com/get_items'
1* Host api.example.com:443 was resolved.
* IPv4: 192.0.2.10
*   Trying 192.0.2.10:443...
2* Connected to api.example.com (192.0.2.10) port 443
3* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
*  subjectAltName: host "api.example.com" matched cert's "api.example.com"
4*  SSL certificate verify ok.
5* ALPN: server accepted http/1.1
6> GET /get_items HTTP/1.1
> Host: api.example.com
> User-Agent: curl/8.7.1
> Accept: */*
>
7< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
8< Content-Type: application/json
< Cache-Control: no-store
<
9{"items":[]}
10* Connection #0 to host api.example.com left intact

1

DNS succeeded: the hostname resolved to an IP address. If resolution fails, check the hostname, DNS configuration and VPN before investigating HTTP.

2

TCP succeeded: curl established a connection to port 443 at that IP. This proves connectivity to a listener, not that the application is healthy. A refusal or timeout here points to the port, listener, routing or firewall.

3

TLS succeeded: the connection is encrypted using TLS 1.3 and the displayed cipher suite. A failure before this point can indicate the wrong protocol/port or a TLS configuration problem.

4

Certificate checks passed: the certificate matches the requested hostname and curl trusts its certificate chain. For a verification error, check the hostname, certificate dates and CA chain rather than bypassing verification with -k.

5

HTTP protocol selected: ALPN (negotiation for http-protocol) negotiated HTTP/1.1. Other servers may select HTTP/2, whose verbose output looks different.

6

Outgoing request (>): curl sends GET /get_items to the indicated host. Check the method, path and headers against what the API expects. Accept: */* allows any response media type; no authorization header is sent in this example. The empty > line ends the request headers.

7

Incoming response (<): 200 OK means the server reports a successful HTTP request. A 3xx with Location indicates a redirect; -v shows it but does not follow it without -L. For 4xx / 5xx, inspect the response body for details.

8

Response headers: the body is declared as JSON, and Cache-Control: no-store tells caches not to store the response. The empty < line separates headers from the body.

9

Response body: the API returned an empty items array. Transport and HTTP succeeded.

10

Connection kept open: curl left the connection available for reuse during this process; this is normal. Lines starting with * are curl’s diagnostic messages.






Reproduce the request

Query parameters




1curl -i --get 'https://api.example.com/users' \
  --data-urlencode 'name=Ada Lovelace' \
  --data-urlencode 'role=admin'

1

use --get so data goes into the URL, not a POST body



JSON — set the request content type and expected response type explicitly




# --data implies POST; no -X POST is needed
curl -i 'https://api.example.com/users' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Accept: application/json' \
  --data '{"name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com"}'

# Send a JSON file without modifying its contents
curl -i -X PUT 'https://api.example.com/users/42' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @user.json
-X changes the method name; it does not configure body handling. Use -I for HEAD. Only run modifying requests against resources you intend to change.

URL-encoded forms versus multipart file uploads




# application/x-www-form-urlencoded; --data-urlencode implies POST
curl -i 'https://api.example.com/form' \
  --data-urlencode 'name=Ada Lovelace' \
  --data-urlencode 'message=a & b'

# multipart/form-data; curl generates the Content-Type and boundary
curl -i 'https://api.example.com/upload' \
  -F 'file=@report.pdf' \
  -F 'description=Monthly report'

Authentication and cookies




# TOKEN must already contain your access token; do not paste secrets into history
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" 'https://api.example.com/me'

# Basic authentication: curl prompts for the password
curl -i --user alice 'https://api.example.com/me'

# Save cookies from one request, then reuse them
curl -i -c cookies.txt 'https://api.example.com/session'
curl -i -b cookies.txt 'https://api.example.com/me'






WarningBe careful wil credentials






Use credentials only over HTTPS and protect cookie files.
Environment variables avoid literal tokens in shell history, but expanded arguments may still be visible to local process inspection.
Do not use --location-trusted to work around redirect authentication issues: it can forward credentials to other hosts.




Avoid combining -X with -L unless you understand how it affects redirected requests.

DNS, connectivity and TLS
# DNS: inspect IPv4 and IPv6 records
dig +short api.example.com A
dig +short api.example.com AAAA

# TCP only: can a connection to this host and port be established?
nc -vz -w 5 api.example.com 443

# Compare IPv4 versus IPv6 connectivity
curl -4 -v 'https://api.example.com/health'
curl -6 -v 'https://api.example.com/health'

# Test a specific server IP while preserving hostname, Host header and TLS SNI
1curl -v --resolve 'api.example.com:443:192.0.2.10' \
  'https://api.example.com/health'

# Inspect the TLS handshake and certificate chain; send the expected SNI hostname
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 \
  -servername api.example.com -showcerts </dev/null

# Trust an internal CA explicitly instead of disabling certificate verification
curl --cacert company-ca.pem 'https://api.example.com/health'

1

--resolve bypasses DNS for that host/port without breaking HTTPS hostname checks.



Proxy or protocol mismatch




# Ignore configured proxies for a direct-connection comparison, if permitted
curl -v --noproxy '*' 'https://api.example.com/health'

# Compare HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 (HTTP/2 requires curl support)
curl -v --http1.1 'https://api.example.com/health'
curl -v --http2 'https://api.example.com/health'
Check environment variables http_proxy, https_proxy, ALL_PROXY and NO_PROXY if requests take an unexpected route. --http2 can fall back to HTTP/1.1; inspect the negotiated protocol in verbose output.


Timeouts, latency and retries
curl -sS -o /dev/null \
  --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \ # <1>
  -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\nIP %{remote_ip}\nDNS %{time_namelookup}s\nConnect %{time_connect}s\nTLS %{time_appconnect}s\nFirst byte %{time_starttransfer}s\nTotal %{time_total}s\n' \
  'https://api.example.com/health'

# Bounded retries for a read-only request after transient failures
curl --fail-with-body --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 20 \
2  --retry 3 --retry-max-time 60 \
  'https://api.example.com/health'

2

--retry handles selected transient failures, not every error, and honors Retry-After where applicable. --retry-max-time limits when another retry may start, not a hard deadline for the entire operation. Do not blindly retry writes: a timeout does not mean the server did not apply the change. Use API-supported idempotency keys or verify the result first.




Browser-only failures (CORS)
If curl succeeds but the browser fails, inspect Developer Tools → Network / Console. Use Copy as cURL to reproduce the actual browser request (remove secrets before sharing). Check cookies, CSRF protection, mixed HTTP/HTTPS content and CORS.


Common errors and likely causes
Curl exit codes describe transfer failures; HTTP status codes describe responses from a server or intermediary. HTTP 000 in curl’s output is not a real status code: no HTTP response status was received.







Symptom
Common causes / next check




curl 5 / 6: could not resolve proxy / host
Typo, wrong DNS, missing VPN or incorrect proxy hostname; check DNS and proxy settings


curl 7: failed to connect
Wrong host/port, no listener, rejected connection or routing/firewall issue; check lsof, nc, container port publishing


curl 28: timeout
Slow DNS, dropped packets, firewall, unreachable upstream or slow application; use verbose output and timings to locate the phase


curl 35: TLS connection error
TLS to a plain HTTP port, unsupported TLS version/cipher, proxy interference or missing client certificate


curl 60: certificate verification failed
Expired certificate, hostname mismatch, untrusted CA, missing intermediate certificate or wrong system clock; fix trust/chain/hostname. -k / --insecure disables verification and is not a production fix


curl 52 / 56: empty reply / receive failure
Peer closed or reset the connection, application crashed, proxy failed or wrong protocol/port; inspect server and proxy logs


Redirect loop / curl 47
Conflicting HTTP↔︎HTTPS redirects, wrong reverse-proxy scheme headers or login/cookie loop; inspect each Location


400 / 422
Malformed JSON, invalid fields, wrong query encoding or schema validation; inspect the error body


401 / 403
Missing/expired token, wrong token audience/scope, insufficient permissions, CSRF or gateway policy; inspect auth headers and logs


404 / 405
Wrong base URL, path, API version or method; check routing, trailing slash and Allow


406 / 415
Unsupported response format (Accept) / request media type (Content-Type); ensure headers match the actual body


409 / 412
State/version conflict or failed precondition (e.g. stale If-Match ETag); fetch current state before retrying


429
Rate limit; honor Retry-After, reduce concurrency and use backoff


500
Application failure; correlate the request ID with server logs


502 / 503 / 504
Upstream failure, unavailable service or gateway timeout; check proxy logs, backend health and timeout settings


200 but HTML instead of JSON
Login redirect, wrong endpoint or proxy error page; inspect redirect history and Content-Type before parsing JSON


Old or unexpected response
Browser/CDN/proxy cache or wrong environment; inspect Age, Cache-Control, ETag and the resolved IP. Try -H 'Cache-Control: no-cache' to request cache revalidation

title: HTTP & REST
text:
REST
Representational State Transfer is an architectural style for resource-oriented systems. HTTP APIs expose resources via URIs and exchange representations (e.g. JSON); JSON over HTTP alone is not REST.

Architectural constraints

Client–server: separate user interface from data storage and processing.
Stateless: each request contains all context needed to process it; no server-side client session is required. Resource state can still be stored.
Cacheable: responses indicate whether/how they can be reused (Cache-Control, validators such as ETag).
Uniform interface: identify resources, manipulate them through representations, use self-descriptive messages and hypermedia links (HATEOAS).
Layered system: clients need not know whether they contact the origin server, a proxy or a gateway.
Code on demand (optional): servers may send executable client code.



CRUD → HTTP methods








Operation
Request
Typical success




Create
POST /users
201 + Location: /users/42


Read
GET /users or GET /users/42
200 + collection/resource


Update
PUT /users/42 (replace), PATCH /users/42 (partial)
200 + resource or 204


Delete
DELETE /users/42
204



PUT can also create at a known URI (201); POST is not limited to CRUD creation.


Resource & query conventions
These are API design conventions, not REST requirements; document and apply them consistently.







Concern
Convention / example




Resource names
Plural nouns, lowercase, hyphens: /users, /order-items; not /getUsers


Identity / relationships
/users/42, /users/42/orders; avoid deep nesting


Filtering
?role=admin&active=true; document operators and multi-value semantics


Sorting
?sort=-created_at,id (descending date, ascending ID); use a unique tie-breaker


Pagination
?limit=20&offset=40 or ?limit=20&cursor=opaque-token; cap page size and return a next-page link/cursor



Offset pagination is simple but can skip/duplicate items as data changes; cursors work better for large/changing collections with stable ordering.


Versioning & HATEOAS

Versioning: reserve new versions for breaking changes; common choices are URI versions (/api/v1/users) or media types (Accept: application/vnd.example.v1+json). Document deprecation and migration timelines.
HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses provide links/actions with relation names (e.g. self, next, cancel), so clients discover valid next steps instead of constructing every URI. Link format depends on the chosen media type.

title: Ansible
text:
Ansible is used to automate tasks and manage infrastructure. It can run the tasks as programs (called modules) on multiple servers with minimal overhead. It is agentless, meaning it does not require any software to be installed on the managed nodes.

Modules

The smallest unit of work in Ansible. They are written in Python and can be used to perform tasks such as installing packages, creating users, and managing services.

Play

A single task that is executed in a specific order on a set of hosts.

Playbooks

A collection of plays that are executed together. Playbooks are written in YAML and can be used to automate complex workflows.

Hosts

A list of servers on which the tasks will be executed.

Inventory

A list of hosts that Ansible will manage. It is written in INI format and can be used to group hosts together.

Roles

A way to organize playbooks and modules. Roles can be used to group related tasks together and can be reused across multiple playbooks.

Ansible Tower

A web-based interface for managing Ansible. It can be used to schedule playbooks, manage inventory, and monitor the status of tasks.

text:
Installation and Setup
Full installation (including dependencies like python packages, ssh, etc.): pipx install --include-deps ansible
Minimal installation: pipx install ansible-core
Installation Guide

title: Ansible
text:
Getting Started
The common folder structure for Ansible is:
.
├── ansible.cfg
├── Inventory
|   └── hosts
├── playbooks
└── roles
    └── common
        ├── tasks
        └── templates
requirements.yml
vault.yml
More info on the concrete files can be found below.

title: Ansible
text:
Inventory Management
The inventory file (often called hosts) is a list of hosts that Ansible will manage. It is written in INI format and can be used to group hosts together.
[webservers]
192.168.1.100
192.168.1.101

[dbservers]
192.168.1.102
192.168.1.103

[reverseproxy]
192.168.1.104
You can call them in the playbook using the hosts keyword and reference complete groups together.

title: Ansible
text:
Writing Playbooks
Playbooks are written in YAML format and are used to define the tasks that Ansible will perform. They are (generally) written in a declarative manner, meaning you define the desired state of the system and Ansible will figure out how to get there. They start with the --- line, followed by the name of the playbook and the hosts that it will run on and variables that will be used..
---
- name: "Hello World Playbook"
  hosts: myserver
  become: true
  vars:
    my_variable: "Hello World"
  tasks: 
   - name: "Print my_variable"
     debug:
       msg: "{{ my_variable }}"
    
   - name: "Install Apache"
     apt:
       name: apache2
       state: present
     when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"

title: Ansible
text:
Roles
Roles are a way to organize playbooks and tasks into reusable units. They are defined in a directory structure and can be included in playbooks using the roles keyword.
Reference a role in a playbook :
---
- name: "Hello World Playbook"
  hosts: myserver
  roles:
    - role: myrole
Define a role:
# roles/myrole/tasks/main.yml
---
- name: "Print my_variable"
  debug:
    msg: "{{ my_variable }}"

title: Ansible
text:
Ansible Galaxy
Ansible Galaxy is a repository for roles. Install roles necessary for the playbooks from ansible galaxy :
ansible-galaxy install -r requirements.yml

title: Ansible
text:
Common Modules

apt/yum
Used to install packages
- name: "Install Apache"
  apt:
    name: apache2


file
Used to manage files and directories. E.g. create, delete, change permissions, etc.
- name: "Create a directory"
  file:
    path: /tmp/mydir
    state: directory
    mode: '0755' # optional, defines the permissions of the file

- name: "Create a file"
  file:
    path: /tmp/myfile
    state: touch
    mode: '0644' 


copy
Used to copy files from the control machine to the managed nodes.
- name: "Copy a file"
  copy:
    src: /tmp/myfile
    dest: /tmp/myfile
    mode: '0644' # optional, defines the permissions of the file


service
Used to manage services. E.g. start, stop, restart, etc.
- name: "Start Apache"
  service:
    name: apache2
    state: started
    enabled: yes

- name: "Stop Apache"
  service:
    name: apache2
    state: stopped
    enabled: no


Docker containers
Used to start a docker container:
- name: "Start myContainer"
      community.docker.docker_container:
        name: myContainer
        image: ghcr.io/theUser/myContainer:latest
        ports:
          - "{{ myContainer_ext_port }}:{{ myContainer_int_port }}"
        env:
          SECRET_API_KEY="{{ vault_myContainer_api_key }}"
        volumes:
          - "/srv/on_server/myContainer:/inContainer/myContainer/cache"
        state: started
        restart_policy: unless-stopped
Used to remove a docker container:
- name: Remove existing myContainer container if present
  community.docker.docker_container:
    name: myContainer
    state: absent

title: Ansible
text:
Variables and Facts
You define variables in the playbook or in a separate file. You can also use facts, which are variables that are automatically gathered from the managed nodes. The variables are defined in the vars section of the playbook and you access them using the { } syntax.
---
- name: "Hello World Playbook"
  hosts: myserver
  vars:
    my_variable: "Hello World"

  ...

  tasks:
    - name: "Print my_variable"
      debug:
        msg: "{{ my_variable }}"
Facts are automatically gathered from the managed nodes and you can access them using the { } syntax.

title: Ansible
text:
Templates
Templates are files that contain variables and are processed by Ansible to generate the final file. They are defined in the templates directory of the role and are referenced using the template module.
Main_variable {{ my_variable }}
Port {{ ssh_port }}
...
Use templates in a playbook:
tasks:
  - name: "Copy template"
    template:
      src: templates/main.conf.j2
      dest: /etc/main.conf

title: Ansible
text:
Conditionals and Loops
You can use conditionals and loops to control the flow of your playbook. Conditionals are defined using the when keyword and loops are defined using the with_items keyword.
tasks:
  - name: "Install Apache"
    apt:
      name: apache2
      state: present
    when: ansible_os_family == "Debian"
    with_items:
      - apache2
      - apache2-utils

title: Ansible
text:
Handlers
Handlers are tasks that are triggered by other tasks. They are defined in the handlers section of the playbook and are referenced using the notify keyword.
tasks:
  - name: "Install Apache"
    apt:
      name: apache2
      state: present
    notify:
      - restart apache
handlers:
  - name: "restart apache"
    service:
      name: apache2
      state: restarted
      enabled: yes

title: Ansible
text:
Best Practices and Tips

Vaults
Vaults are used to encrypt sensitive data in your playbooks. They are defined using the ansible-vault command.
To encrypt a file:
ansible-vault encrypt secret.yml
To edit a file:
ansible-vault edit secret.yml
To reference a file in a playbook:
- name
  ...

  tasks:
    - name: "include vault variables"
     include_vars:
       file: ../secret.yml

title: Ansible
text:
Troubleshooting

Debugging
To debug a playbook, you can use the debug module.
tasks:
  - name: "Debug"
    debug:
      msg: "Hello World"
run a playbook in debug mode:
ansible-playbook playbook.yml -vvv


Force execution of all tasks
To force execution of all tasks, you can use the --force-handlers option.
ansible-playbook playbook.yml --force-handlers
