Helm packages Kubernetes resource templates into a chart and fills them with settings from values.yaml when installing or upgrading a release. This example runs one Shiny application pod through a Deployment, which recreates the pod if it is deleted; a separate bare Pod manifest is therefore unnecessary.
Assume a suitable Dockerfile already exists: the image must support OpenShift’s arbitrary non-root UID and the application must listen on 0.0.0.0:3838. The cluster must be able to pull the image; a private registry additionally requires image-pull credentials. No ImageStream is required when referencing an image directly.
File structure:
deploy/
├── project.yaml                 # Create separately before installing the chart
└── shiny/                       # Helm chart
    ├── Chart.yaml               # Chart metadata
    ├── values.yaml              # Default settings
    └── templates/
        ├── deployment.yaml      # Pod template and replica management
        ├── pvc.yaml             # Persistent application storage
        └── service.yaml         # Stable internal network endpoint


deploy/project.yaml stays outside the chart so uninstalling the release does not delete the project:
1apiVersion: project.openshift.io/v1
kind: Project
metadata:
2  name: shiny-demo

1

Project is the OpenShift equivalent of a Kubernetes namespace. It has to be created before the Helm release.

2

name identifies the project and must match the namespace passed to Helm with --namespace.


Creating a Project typically requires administrator rights.



deploy/shiny/Chart.yaml:
1apiVersion: v2
name: shiny
2version: 0.1.0

1

apiVersion: v2 uses the chart format supported by Helm 3 and later.

2

version is the chart’s package version. It is independent of the application’s image tag.





deploy/shiny/values.yaml:
image:
1  repository: quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny
  tag: "1.0.0"
2replicaCount: 1
3containerPort: 3838
service:
4  port: 3838
persistence:
5  size: 5Gi
  mountPath: /data
resources:
6  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
7  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi

1

image identifies the registry image to build and push before deployment.

2

replicaCount sets the number of application pods maintained by the Deployment.

3

containerPort must match the actual listening port of the application and does not configure the application itself.

4

service.port sets the port exposed by the internal Service. It can be different from the container port.

5

persistence requests 5 GiB of storage and mounts it at /data, where the application must explicitly write files that should survive pod replacement.

6

requests tells the scheduler to account for 0.1 CPU and 256 MiB of memory per container when placing the pod.

7

limits caps CPU usage at one CPU through throttling and sets a 1 GiB memory limit, exceeding which can cause the container to be OOM-killed.


These resource sizes are examples and should be adjusted to measured application needs and project quotas.



deploy/shiny/templates/pvc.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
1kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
2  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}-data"
spec:
  accessModes:
3    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
4      storage: "{{ .Values.persistence.size }}"

1

A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests persistent storage from the cluster rather than using the container’s ephemeral writable layer.

2

The release-specific name connects this claim to the Deployment’s volume reference.

3

ReadWriteOnce permits read-write mounting on one node at a time, not necessarily by only one pod.

4

storage requests the capacity configured in values.yaml, using the cluster’s default StorageClass because storageClassName is omitted.


This example assumes a default StorageClass with dynamic provisioning; otherwise, add spec.storageClassName for a suitable class or arrange a matching pre-provisioned volume with your administrator. Keep replicaCount: 1 for this single-writer example rather than scaling multiple pods against the same claim.
The mounted volume has its own permissions, replacing the image directory’s permissions; the storage driver and OpenShift’s allowed group settings must permit the assigned non-root user to write to it. Do not hard-code a UID or fsGroup outside the project’s allowed ranges.






Data survives pod replacement, but this chart manages the PVC, so helm uninstall also deletes the claim and may delete the underlying storage depending on its reclaim policy; arrange backups and a deliberate retention policy for important data.






deploy/shiny/templates/deployment.yaml:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
1  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
spec:
2  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  strategy:
3    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
4      app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
5  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: shiny
6          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - name: http
7              containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
8              port: http
9          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "{{ .Values.resources.requests.cpu }}"
              memory: "{{ .Values.resources.requests.memory }}"
            limits:
              cpu: "{{ .Values.resources.limits.cpu }}"
              memory: "{{ .Values.resources.limits.memory }}"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
10              mountPath: "{{ .Values.persistence.mountPath }}"
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
11            claimName: "{{ .Release.Name }}-data"

1

.Release.Name is supplied by Helm, so installing the release as shiny names the Deployment shiny.

2

.Values reads settings from values.yaml, optionally overridden with Helm’s -f or --set options.

3

Recreate stops the old pod before creating its replacement during an update, avoiding overlapping writers and cross-node volume-attachment conflicts at the cost of downtime.

4

selector.matchLabels identifies the Deployment’s pods and must match the labels under template.metadata.labels.

5

template defines the pods created by the Deployment, including their labels and container configuration.

6

image references the prebuilt registry image, whose default entrypoint and command start the application.

7

The named http port documents the container’s listening port and lets the Service reference it by name.

8

readinessProbe checks HTTP / and allows the pod to receive Service traffic only after the check succeeds.

9

resources applies the configured requests and limits to each application container, with explicit quotes keeping resource quantities as YAML strings.

10

volumeMounts exposes the pod’s data volume at the configured path inside the container.

11

volumes connects the pod’s data volume to the PVC created by this release.


No fixed runAsUser is set, allowing OpenShift to assign a UID permitted by the project’s security policy.



deploy/shiny/templates/service.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
1  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
spec:
2  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
3    app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
4      targetPort: http

1

The Service uses the release name as its stable DNS name within the project.

2

ClusterIP exposes the application inside the cluster rather than publishing a port on your computer or an external hostname.

3

selector sends traffic to ready pods with the matching app label.

4

port is the Service’s listening port and targetPort forwards traffic to the pod’s named http port.





Run these steps from the directory containing deploy/ and your Dockerfile:

Build and push the image: run docker build -t quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny:1.0.0 . followed by docker push quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny:1.0.0, using the same repository and tag as in values.yaml.
Log in and provision the project: Have your admin login and run oc apply -f deploy/project.yaml.
Check the chart locally: run helm lint ./deploy/shiny and helm template shiny ./deploy/shiny --namespace shiny-demo to inspect the generated manifests without deploying them.
Install or update: run helm upgrade --install shiny ./deploy/shiny --namespace shiny-demo --wait --timeout 5m; Helm loads the chart’s values.yaml automatically and waits for the workload to become ready.
Inspect the workload and storage: run oc get pods,services,pvc -n shiny-demo and oc logs -f deployment/shiny -n shiny-demo; if storage remains Pending after a pod is scheduled, inspect oc describe pvc shiny-data -n shiny-demo for provisioning or binding errors.
Test locally: run oc port-forward service/shiny 3838:3838 -n shiny-demo and open http://localhost:3838 while the command is running.

For a persistent external HTTP(S) endpoint, add an OpenShift Route pointing to this Service; port-forwarding is only a temporary local connection. If the application needs credentials, create a Kubernetes Secret in the same project outside the chart; keep actual secret values out of values.yaml and Git.
See the Helm chart documentation for chart structure and templating.






Nodes

Physical or virtual machines running containerized workloads. Support various runtime classes and compute profiles. Can be managed through machine sets and autoscaling.

Clusters

Distributed systems for container orchestration. Support hybrid and multi-cloud deployments and advanced networking models.

Service mesh

Infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication. Provides traffic management, security, and observability features.

Show node resource usage
oc adm top nodes


List machine sets
oc get machinesets -n openshift-machine-api


Show installed cluster version and update channel
oc get clusterversion


List operators and their health
oc get clusteroperators

Helm packages Kubernetes resource templates into a chart and fills them with settings from values.yaml when installing or upgrading a release. This example runs one Shiny application pod through a Deployment, which recreates the pod if it is deleted; a separate bare Pod manifest is therefore unnecessary.
Assume a suitable Dockerfile already exists: the image must support OpenShift’s arbitrary non-root UID and the application must listen on 0.0.0.0:3838. The cluster must be able to pull the image; a private registry additionally requires image-pull credentials. No ImageStream is required when referencing an image directly.
File structure:
deploy/
├── project.yaml                 # Create separately before installing the chart
└── shiny/                       # Helm chart
    ├── Chart.yaml               # Chart metadata
    ├── values.yaml              # Default settings
    └── templates/
        ├── deployment.yaml      # Pod template and replica management
        ├── pvc.yaml             # Persistent application storage
        └── service.yaml         # Stable internal network endpoint


deploy/project.yaml stays outside the chart so uninstalling the release does not delete the project:
1apiVersion: project.openshift.io/v1
kind: Project
metadata:
2  name: shiny-demo

1

Project is the OpenShift equivalent of a Kubernetes namespace. It has to be created before the Helm release.

2

name identifies the project and must match the namespace passed to Helm with --namespace.


Creating a Project typically requires administrator rights.



deploy/shiny/Chart.yaml:
1apiVersion: v2
name: shiny
2version: 0.1.0

1

apiVersion: v2 uses the chart format supported by Helm 3 and later.

2

version is the chart’s package version. It is independent of the application’s image tag.





deploy/shiny/values.yaml:
image:
1  repository: quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny
  tag: "1.0.0"
2replicaCount: 1
3containerPort: 3838
service:
4  port: 3838
persistence:
5  size: 5Gi
  mountPath: /data
resources:
6  requests:
    cpu: 100m
    memory: 256Mi
7  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 1Gi

1

image identifies the registry image to build and push before deployment.

2

replicaCount sets the number of application pods maintained by the Deployment.

3

containerPort must match the actual listening port of the application and does not configure the application itself.

4

service.port sets the port exposed by the internal Service. It can be different from the container port.

5

persistence requests 5 GiB of storage and mounts it at /data, where the application must explicitly write files that should survive pod replacement.

6

requests tells the scheduler to account for 0.1 CPU and 256 MiB of memory per container when placing the pod.

7

limits caps CPU usage at one CPU through throttling and sets a 1 GiB memory limit, exceeding which can cause the container to be OOM-killed.


These resource sizes are examples and should be adjusted to measured application needs and project quotas.



deploy/shiny/templates/pvc.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
1kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
2  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}-data"
spec:
  accessModes:
3    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
4      storage: "{{ .Values.persistence.size }}"

1

A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) requests persistent storage from the cluster rather than using the container’s ephemeral writable layer.

2

The release-specific name connects this claim to the Deployment’s volume reference.

3

ReadWriteOnce permits read-write mounting on one node at a time, not necessarily by only one pod.

4

storage requests the capacity configured in values.yaml, using the cluster’s default StorageClass because storageClassName is omitted.


This example assumes a default StorageClass with dynamic provisioning; otherwise, add spec.storageClassName for a suitable class or arrange a matching pre-provisioned volume with your administrator. Keep replicaCount: 1 for this single-writer example rather than scaling multiple pods against the same claim.
The mounted volume has its own permissions, replacing the image directory’s permissions; the storage driver and OpenShift’s allowed group settings must permit the assigned non-root user to write to it. Do not hard-code a UID or fsGroup outside the project’s allowed ranges.






Data survives pod replacement, but this chart manages the PVC, so helm uninstall also deletes the claim and may delete the underlying storage depending on its reclaim policy; arrange backups and a deliberate retention policy for important data.






deploy/shiny/templates/deployment.yaml:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
1  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
spec:
2  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  strategy:
3    type: Recreate
  selector:
    matchLabels:
4      app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
5  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: shiny
6          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          ports:
            - name: http
7              containerPort: {{ .Values.containerPort }}
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /
8              port: http
9          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "{{ .Values.resources.requests.cpu }}"
              memory: "{{ .Values.resources.requests.memory }}"
            limits:
              cpu: "{{ .Values.resources.limits.cpu }}"
              memory: "{{ .Values.resources.limits.memory }}"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
10              mountPath: "{{ .Values.persistence.mountPath }}"
      volumes:
        - name: data
          persistentVolumeClaim:
11            claimName: "{{ .Release.Name }}-data"

1

.Release.Name is supplied by Helm, so installing the release as shiny names the Deployment shiny.

2

.Values reads settings from values.yaml, optionally overridden with Helm’s -f or --set options.

3

Recreate stops the old pod before creating its replacement during an update, avoiding overlapping writers and cross-node volume-attachment conflicts at the cost of downtime.

4

selector.matchLabels identifies the Deployment’s pods and must match the labels under template.metadata.labels.

5

template defines the pods created by the Deployment, including their labels and container configuration.

6

image references the prebuilt registry image, whose default entrypoint and command start the application.

7

The named http port documents the container’s listening port and lets the Service reference it by name.

8

readinessProbe checks HTTP / and allows the pod to receive Service traffic only after the check succeeds.

9

resources applies the configured requests and limits to each application container, with explicit quotes keeping resource quantities as YAML strings.

10

volumeMounts exposes the pod’s data volume at the configured path inside the container.

11

volumes connects the pod’s data volume to the PVC created by this release.


No fixed runAsUser is set, allowing OpenShift to assign a UID permitted by the project’s security policy.



deploy/shiny/templates/service.yaml:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
1  name: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
spec:
2  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
3    app: "{{ .Release.Name }}"
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: {{ .Values.service.port }}
4      targetPort: http

1

The Service uses the release name as its stable DNS name within the project.

2

ClusterIP exposes the application inside the cluster rather than publishing a port on your computer or an external hostname.

3

selector sends traffic to ready pods with the matching app label.

4

port is the Service’s listening port and targetPort forwards traffic to the pod’s named http port.





Run these steps from the directory containing deploy/ and your Dockerfile:

Build and push the image: run docker build -t quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny:1.0.0 . followed by docker push quay.io/MY_COMPANY/shiny:1.0.0, using the same repository and tag as in values.yaml.
Log in and provision the project: Have your admin login and run oc apply -f deploy/project.yaml.
Check the chart locally: run helm lint ./deploy/shiny and helm template shiny ./deploy/shiny --namespace shiny-demo to inspect the generated manifests without deploying them.
Install or update: run helm upgrade --install shiny ./deploy/shiny --namespace shiny-demo --wait --timeout 5m; Helm loads the chart’s values.yaml automatically and waits for the workload to become ready.
Inspect the workload and storage: run oc get pods,services,pvc -n shiny-demo and oc logs -f deployment/shiny -n shiny-demo; if storage remains Pending after a pod is scheduled, inspect oc describe pvc shiny-data -n shiny-demo for provisioning or binding errors.
Test locally: run oc port-forward service/shiny 3838:3838 -n shiny-demo and open http://localhost:3838 while the command is running.

For a persistent external HTTP(S) endpoint, add an OpenShift Route pointing to this Service; port-forwarding is only a temporary local connection. If the application needs credentials, create a Kubernetes Secret in the same project outside the chart; keep actual secret values out of values.yaml and Git.
See the Helm chart documentation for chart structure and templating.

title: Pytest
text:
Best practices

Arrange → Act → Assert; one behavior per test, with descriptive names.
Test observable behavior, not implementation details; cover normal, boundary, and failure cases.
Keep tests independent, deterministic, and fast: no ordering dependencies, real network calls in unit tests, or arbitrary sleeps.
Mock external boundaries, not everything; use integration tests to verify real interactions.
Prefer small, explicit fixtures over hidden autouse setup; always clean up resources.
Run tests in CI. Optional: pytest-cov adds --cov=myapp --cov-branch --cov-report=term-missing; coverage reveals gaps, not correctness.

title: Pytest
text:
Assertions & exceptions
Use plain assert; pytest shows the values involved when it fails.
import pytest

def test_assertions():
    assert 2 + 2 == 4
    assert "py" in "pytest"
    assert [1, 2] == [1, 2]          # Compare contents, not identity
    assert None is None            # Use `is None`, not `== None`
    assert 0.1 + 0.2 == pytest.approx(0.3)

def test_invalid_input():
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="invalid literal"):
        int("hello")               # `match` is a regex

text:
Fixtures: setup & cleanup
Fixtures are reusable functions that prepare data or resources for tests and can clean them up afterward. Tests request fixtures by argument name. Put shared fixtures in tests/conftest.py; pytest discovers them automatically—no import needed.
import sqlite3
import pytest

@pytest.fixture
def db():
    connection = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    try:
        yield connection           # Setup before yield; cleanup after
    finally:
        connection.close()

def test_database(db):
    assert db.execute("SELECT 1").fetchone() == (1,)
Default scope is function (fresh per test). Other scopes: class, module, package, session. Share expensive resources carefully; avoid shared mutable state.

title: Pytest
text:
Mocking
Mocking temporarily replaces real objects or functions with simpler substitutes so tests can isolate behavior without relying on external systems and run faster. Install pytest-mock to use its mocker fixture:
uv add --dev pytest-mock

Example:
Application code in config.py imports expanduser to build a config path:
# config.py
from os.path import expanduser
from pathlib import Path

def config_path():
    return Path(expanduser("~")) / "settings.toml"
Tests in tests/test_config.py patch the imported name in config, not its original definition in os.path:
# tests/test_config.py
import pytest
from config import config_path

1def test_config_path(tmp_path, mocker):
    # Arrange / Given: a controlled home directory
2    home = mocker.patch("config.expanduser",
3        autospec=True,
4        return_value=str(tmp_path),
    )
    # Act / When: build the config path
    result = config_path()

    # Assert / Then: the path uses that directory
    assert result == tmp_path / "settings.toml"
5    home.assert_called_once_with("~")

def test_config_path_failure(mocker):
    # Arrange / Given: home directory lookup fails
    mocker.patch("config.expanduser", autospec=True,
6        side_effect=TimeoutError("offline"),
    )
    # Assert / Then: expect the lookup error to propagate
    with pytest.raises(TimeoutError, match="offline"):
        # Act / When: build the config path
        config_path()

1

The mocker fixture provides patching helpers and automatically undoes patches after each test; mocker.spy(object, "method") instead records calls while keeping the real implementation.

2

Patch config.expanduser because config_path looks up that name in config; patching os.path.expanduser would not replace the reference already imported by from os.path import expanduser.

3

autospec=True makes the mock enforce the original function’s parameter signature, so calling the patched expanduser with missing or unexpected arguments raises TypeError instead of silently accepting an invalid call; it does not check argument types or run the real function.

4

return_value makes the patched function return the supplied value, here the test’s temporary directory instead of the real home directory.

5

Verify that the patched function was called exactly once with "~".

6

side_effect makes the patched function raise the supplied exception to simulate a failure.

@pytest.mark.skip(reason="Feature not available")

@pytest.mark.xfail(reason="Known bug #123", strict=True)
def test_known_bug():

testpaths = ["tests"]
addopts = "-ra --strict-markers"
markers = ["integration: tests involving external systems"]

Concepts

Projects: You can manage packages project-wide using uv commands and the project.toml file.
Scripts: You can also manage packages for independent scripts using uv commands using the script-header in a python script.
Scripts: You can also manage packages for independent scripts using uv commands using the script-header in a python script.
Tools: To run packages as commandline tools, you can use special uv commands.



Installation

Install uv




pipx install uv

Upgrade uv




uv self update


Python Versions
Manage Python installations and versions.

Install Python versions




uv python install 3.9.7

List available Python versions




uv python list

Find an installed Python version




uv python find 3.9

Pin a project to a specific Python version




uv python pin 3.9.7

Uninstall a Python version




uv python uninstall 3.9.7


Scripts
Execute and manage dependencies in standalone Python scripts. The script needs to contain a script header.

script header




# /// script
# dependencies = [
#   "requests<3",
#   "rich",
# ]
# ///

import requests
from rich import print
...

Run a script




uv run example.py

Add a dependency to a script




uv add --script SomePackage

Remove a dependency from a script




uv remove --script SomePackage


Projects
Create and manage depencies of whole projects with a pyproject.toml file.

Create a new project with a pyproject.toml file and a virtual environment




uv init

Add a dependency to the project




uv add SomePackage

Remove a dependency from the project




uv remove SomePackage

Sync project dependencies with the virtual environment




uv sync

Create a lockfile for dependencies




uv lock

Run a command in the project environment




uv run python script.py

View the dependency tree




uv tree


Tools
Install and manage tools from Python package indexes.

Run a tool in a temporary environment




uvx ruff

Install a tool user-wide




uv tool install black

Uninstall a tool




uv tool uninstall black

List installed tools




uv tool list

Update the shell to include tool executables




uv tool update-shell
